summary_plain: The Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II) investigation studied how different solid materials burn and spread flames in microgravity using a small wind tunnel inside the International Space Station. Researchers burned fuels like wax, fabrics, and plastics under various airflow and oxygen conditions to understand fire behavior in space. These findings help engineers improve spacecraft fire safety systems and refine computer models used to predict fire risks both in space and on Earth.
summary_expert: BASS-II performed tests aboard the International Space Station using the Microgravity Science Glovebox flow duct hardware, executing 129 tests across multiple solid fuels including Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA, and SIBAL. Sample geometries tested comprised candles, fabrics, rods, slabs, spheres, and thin films. The primary variables investigated were forced flow velocity, ambient oxygen concentration ranging from 14 to 22 percent (mole fraction 0.14 to 0.22), fuel type, thickness, and geometry under opposed and concurrent flow conditions. The documents provided describe the objectives, experimental design, and hardware capabilities, yielding data to study ignition, flame spread, extinction limits, and to support computational combustion models.

key_findings.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests using solid fuels including Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA, and SIBAL in candle, fabric, rod, slab, sphere, and thin film geometries.
The oxygen concentration in BASS-II tests ranged from 14 to 22 percent (mole fraction 0.14 to 0.22).
In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth.
